project.name: Not Arbitrary 04 — The Treble Clef Is a Letter G

entries.speaker: Narrator
entries.text: The curl at the start of a line of music is not a symbol. It is a letter, written badly for nine hundred years. This is what was left.
entries.direction: Warm, unhurried, opening a story. The last clause is the hook — land it plainly, no wink.

entries.speaker: Narrator
entries.text: Before the stave, a scribe drew the shape of a melody above the words. It told a singer the tune went up. It never told him how far. So a monk in Arezzo ruled lines across the page.
entries.direction: Conversational, as if sketching while speaking. A small beat of dryness on how far.

entries.speaker: Narrator
entries.text: But one ruled line looks like every other. So he wrote a letter at the head of one, to say which note it was, and inked one line red and another yellow.
entries.direction: Practical and clear, building through the sentence.

entries.speaker: Narrator
entries.text: He called those letters litterae clavis. The key letters. Which is all the word clef has ever meant.
entries.direction: Say the Latin phrase litterae clavis plainly, with a clear short i in the first syllable of litterae, and let it finish before the English. Then a small, satisfied landing on the last sentence.

entries.speaker: Narrator
entries.text: Then music started climbing. When a tune went above the letters already in use, a scribe reached for the next one along, and put a capital G at the head of its line.
entries.direction: Light and moving. Give the capital G its full weight, do not swallow it.

entries.speaker: Narrator
entries.text: He wrote it ten thousand times. A hand that writes the same letter that often stops lifting the pen. It is only what happens to a letter that is never drawn slowly.
entries.direction: Reflective, slowing. The last sentence is the idea of the whole film — let it sit.

entries.speaker: Narrator
entries.text: Nine hundred years of not lifting the pen. And it still winds around the line it was put there to name.
entries.direction: Quiet satisfaction. Short. Let the final phrase rest.

entries.speaker: Narrator
entries.text: The letter on the red line came out unrecognisable. Its arms did not survive. What replaced them was a dot above the line and a dot below, so nobody could mistake the line.
entries.direction: Brisker than the previous shots — this one moves. Dry on did not survive.

entries.speaker: Narrator
entries.text: Those marks tell you where you are. The two that tell you what to play are letters as well. And they are the same letter.
entries.direction: A turn. Set the first two sentences down cleanly, pause, then the last one as a small provocation.

entries.speaker: Narrator
entries.text: In the medieval scale, exactly one note could be sung two ways. They called the lower one b rotundum. A scribe wrote it as the letter b, with a round bowl.
entries.direction: Curious and steady. Say the Latin phrase b rotundum plainly and finish it before the next sentence begins.

entries.speaker: Narrator
entries.text: It barely had to change at all. Which is why, in Germany, the letter B still means the flat one, and nobody there finds that strange.
entries.direction: Warm, a little amused. Give the letter B its full weight.

entries.speaker: Narrator
entries.text: The higher of the two had to look different, or a singer would sing the wrong note. So they squared the bowl off. They called it b quadratum.
entries.direction: Matter of fact, one step at a time. Say the Latin phrase b quadratum plainly, at the very end, and let it finish.

entries.speaker: Narrator
entries.text: A sharp is that square. So is a natural. Two of the most common marks in music, and both of them are one letter that nobody could be bothered to round off.
entries.direction: Deliberate. The first two sentences are short and flat on purpose; the last one opens out.

entries.speaker: Narrator
entries.text: Nothing on that page was designed. Every mark there is handwriting, worn down by a thousand years of copying. And the letters themselves had been pictures once.
entries.direction: Slower, laying things down one at a time. The last sentence is an aside, thrown away lightly.

entries.speaker: Narrator
entries.text: You never learned a new set of symbols. You learned three letters, drawn by people in a hurry. You have known the alphabet all along.
entries.direction: Warm close, slowing into the final line. Keep the last sentence simple and unhurried.
